chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn Idris (may Allah be pleased with him) told us, saying: My father told us, from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari, from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Nufali, from al-Husayn ibn al-Mukhtar, with his chain, he elevated it, saying:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his Family) said: Cursed, cursed is the one who is a 'Akmat A'ma (a specific type of blind person or metaphorical figure), cursed, cursed is the one who is the 'Abd al-Dinar wa al-Dirham (slave of the dinar and dirham), cursed, cursed is the one who married a beast.

key_terms.أَكْمَةِ أَعْمَى: Akmat A'ma (a specific type of blind person or metaphorical figure)
key_terms.عَبْدَ الدِّينَارِ وَالدِّرْهَمِ: Abd al-Dinar wa al-Dirham (slave of the dinar and dirham, i.e., enslaved by wealth)
key_terms.نَكَحَ بِهِيْمَةً: Nakaha bi-haymah (married a beast, i.e., bestiality)

ai.seo_question: What are the three groups mentioned as cursed in this hadith from Mani al-Akhbar?
ai.summary: In *Mani al-Akhbar*, Shaykh al-Saduq records this hadith emphasizing three distinct forms of spiritual and physical corruption: the 'Akmat A'ma, often interpreted by Shia scholars as a metaphor for those blinded by ignorance or specific figures like the Umayyads, the 'Abd al-Dinar wa al-Dirham representing those enslaved by materialism, and the practitioner of bestiality. This triad illustrates the progression from intellectual blindness to economic enslavement and finally to unnatural acts, serving as a comprehensive critique of societal decay in early Islamic history.
